title: The Desert Hospital That Was Going Broke Until It Was Paid in Advance
dek: In the Depression a young surgeon's fee-for-service hospital for aqueduct workers was failing, until an insurer offered to pay him up front.

story.event: Switching a failing fee-for-service desert hospital to prepayment for Colorado River Aqueduct workers
story.summary: In 1933 the surgeon Sidney Garfield built Contractors General Hospital near Desert Center, California, on borrowed money to treat Colorado River Aqueduct workers, but on fee-for-service it was soon near bankruptcy. Harold Hatch of Industrial Indemnity Exchange proposed paying him a fixed share of insurance premiums in advance, other insurers followed, and workers bought a voluntary plan for other illness at five cents a day. Paid for health rather than injury, Garfield turned to prevention, and the model later became Kaiser Permanente.
paragraphs: In 1933, with private practice in Los Angeles all but "nonexistent", as he later put it, the young surgeon Sidney Garfield went looking for somewhere his skills were needed. An intern friend from Indio told him about the Colorado River Aqueduct: some five thousand men strung across 115 miles of desert, building a channel to carry water to Los Angeles, with no medical care nearer than Indio. The Metropolitan Water District offered him $175 a month as a staff doctor. He thought it too little and decided to build his own.

With $2,500 in cash, borrowed money and equipment advanced by suppliers, he put up Contractors General Hospital, about six miles west of Desert Center: plain outside, air-conditioned within. His partner soon dropped out, and Garfield slept on a folding cot in the office. Charging fee-for-service, the hospital struggled from the start. The workers could not pay. Insurers sent his bills back discounted, complaining of too much care, and moved serious cases to Los Angeles once the men were stable. Within a few months, he recalled, it looked as if they would go broke.

The way out came from Harold Hatch, manager of Industrial Indemnity Exchange, an insurer part-owned by the contractor Henry Kaiser. Hatch suggested paying Garfield a fixed share of premiums, 12.5 per cent, in advance, so nobody had to argue over bills. It was more than he was earning; "I had nothing to lose," he said. The other insurers agreed to the same terms, worth by his reckoning about eight cents per worker per day, and the contractors sold their men a voluntary plan for illness off the job at five cents a day.

Steady money changed more than the accounts. Before, Garfield admitted, the hospital had depended on men getting hurt: "It was embarrassing to me to want people to get hurt." Now it did better when they stayed well. When nail punctures piled up from one job, his team got the nails cleared; where head injuries clustered, tunnels were shored up. By the end of the five-year job he had built and paid for three small hospitals. In 1938 Henry Kaiser's son Edgar asked him to run medical care at Grand Coulee Dam, and the arrangement he took north grew into Kaiser Permanente.

quote.text: So in order to claim the aid of truth, selfishness has to be unselfish to some extent.
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Garfield was not setting out to reform medicine; he was trying not to go broke, and said so. Tagore argues that even self-interest, to succeed, must reach beyond itself. The prepaid contract made that literal: the hospital now survived on the workers' health.

reflection: How you are paid shapes what you notice. Garfield was not a worse doctor before prepayment; he was a doctor whose income arrived with each injury, and he felt that pull clearly enough to be embarrassed by it.

It is worth asking, without blame, what your own arrangements quietly reward: the busy day over the quiet one, the visible rescue over the problem that never happened. A great deal of good work leaves nothing to show for itself. Garfield needed a new contract before he could see that. You may only need to look honestly at last week.
invitation: Pick one thing your work is measured or judged by. Write down one good outcome it never counts, such as a problem that was prevented, and mention it to one colleague today.

research_notes: Payment figures differ. Garfield's oral history (1986) says Industrial Indemnity paid 12.5 per cent of premiums, which he reckoned at about eight cents per member per day, and that the voluntary non-industrial plan was five cents a day; Kaiser Permanente's history page gives the same five cents for workers and an unstated fixed amount from the insurer; Jay Crosson (Permanente Journal, 2006) says the enterprise collected 'a dime a day' from about 5,000 workers, possibly the two payments combined; San Diego Jewish World gives five cents for work accidents plus another nickel for other illness, which conflicts with Garfield's account that the insurers paid for work injuries. The story uses Garfield's own figures and attributes them to him. Garfield also says the insurers later raised the share to 22 per cent unasked; the story omits this. Hatch's role: Kaiser Permanente's page says Henry Kaiser sent Hatch to Garfield, while Garfield says he did not know Kaiser then and that Hatch, the insurer's manager, made the suggestion while visiting; the story follows Garfield and notes only that Kaiser was a part-owner of the insurer, which Garfield states. San Diego Jewish World repeats a story of Hatch arriving with an injured Henry Kaiser but itself calls it lore; not used. Bed count: Garfield says fifteen, Gilford twelve, so the story gives none. The $2,500: Garfield says he had $2,500 in cash; Gilford and San Diego Jewish World say it was borrowed from his father; the story says 'with $2,500 in cash, borrowed money'. The prevention examples (nails, tunnels) are Garfield's; Kaiser Permanente credits Garfield and the nurse Betty Runyen with clean worksites and hard hats. The year of the Grand Coulee move, 1938, comes from the oral history's chronology. The PubMed Central pages sometimes serve a browser check to scripted requests; they loaded for the source checker. Tagore wrote Sadhana in English, so no translator is given.
